note: Synthetic transcript written for evaluation; not a real person's words.
setting: Family compound house (abusua fie) shared by many households in Asawase, Kumasi, Ghana, childhood until 1994

turns.speaker: B
turns.transcript: Okay, so tell me about the house.

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: It was our abusua fie, the family house, in Asawase, in Kumasi. I lived there from small until, eh, 1994 maybe, when we moved to Accra. A big compound house. Many families. My grandfather built it, in the sixties I think, or he started it and his brothers finished.

turns.speaker: B
turns.transcript: What did it look like from the street?

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: From the street it was just a long wall, cement, painted, eh, cream? Cream, with brown at the bottom. And the gutter in front, the open drain, you had to jump over it or walk on the slab. Then one entrance in the middle, a passage. No gate, just a passage through the building to the inside.

turns.speaker: B
turns.transcript: And inside?

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: Inside is the adiwo, the open courtyard. Everything happens there. Cooking, washing, the children playing ampe, funerals even. All the rooms face into it, around, like a square. Our room, my mother's room, was on the left as you come out of the passage. Second door. No, third. The first was Auntie Akosua's, then Mr. Boateng the tailor, then us.

turns.speaker: B
turns.transcript: How big was your room?

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: Small. One room for my mother, me and my two brothers. Maybe ten feet by twelve. My mother had the big bed, and we boys slept on mats on the floor. A wardrobe, and a chest where she kept her things for occasions.

turns.speaker: B
turns.transcript: Where was the bed, in the room?

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: Against the back wall, eh, the wall opposite the door. The wardrobe just beside the door. That's all, there was no space for anything else.

turns.speaker: B
turns.transcript: Where did people cook?

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: In the adiwo mostly, on coal pots. Everybody had their own coal pot outside their door. There was a kitchen room too, at the back, on the right side, but it was smoky, only my grandmother used it, on Sundays.

turns.speaker: B
turns.transcript: And water?

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: There was a well. No, sorry, I'm mixing it up with my uncle's place in Suame, the well was there. We had a standpipe, a tap, in the middle of the adiwo, but the water didn't always flow, so we stored it. Two big drums by our door. And the ahina, the clay pot for drinking water, that one was inside our room, in the corner, it kept the water cool.

turns.speaker: B
turns.transcript: Was there a bathroom?

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: The bathhouse, yes, at the back, in the left corner. Cement, open on top. You carried your water in with you. And the toilet, the KVIP, was apart from it, behind my grandfather's room, you went through a small gap beside his room. At night nobody wanted to go there.

turns.speaker: B
turns.transcript: Your grandfather had a room at the back?

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: In the middle at the back, the biggest room, facing the passage, so he could see who came in and who went out. He had a radio, a big Philips, on a shelf above his bed, and the whole compound listened to the football through his door. Kotoko. He turned it up so loud.

turns.speaker: B
turns.transcript: Were there trees?

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: One mango tree. Not in the adiwo, it was outside, along the side of the house, by Mr. Boateng's room. So the left. Outside, on the left. Mangoes everywhere in the season, and the fights over them.

turns.speaker: B
turns.transcript: Anything else in the courtyard?

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: A long wooden bench outside grandfather's door, where the old men sat. Clotheslines across, from corner to corner. Oh, and a small cement platform, a raised bit, near the standpipe, where the women washed. We just called it the washing place.

turns.speaker: B
turns.transcript: How big was the courtyard?

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: Hmm. Big enough for a funeral, a hundred people sitting. In feet I can't really say. Maybe forty feet long. The width less, I don't know.

turns.speaker: B
turns.transcript: And the front, either side of the passage?

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: On the right of the passage, the room at the front was a shop, a provision shop, my uncle's wife ran it, with a window, a hatch, opening onto the street. On the left of the passage a room for a lodger, a student from the Tech, KNUST. I don't remember him well, he was always studying.

turns.speaker: B
turns.transcript: And the roof, what kind was it?

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: Zinc. Aluminium sheets, the corrugated ones, and when it rained you couldn't hear anything, you had to shout. The roof was only over the rooms. The adiwo was open, of course.
